Cerebral palsy: Nutritional aspects


Growth
Adequacy of growth may be the single most valuable indicator of nutritional status in children. Healthy, typically developing chil-
dren grow at predictable rates, with patterns reﬂective of certain age categories. Children with CP have altered growth patterns and
tend to be shorter and lighter than the reference standard (Day et al., 2007). Growth patterns can be affected by gender, age, pubertal

Factors affecting nutritional status.
• Associated disabilities
• Required physical and cognitive support
• Oral motor dysfunction/dysphagia
• Increased or decreased energy needs
• Abnormal tone and motor patterns
• Food refusal/selectivity
• Behavioral problems
• Psychosocial needs
• GI issues – emesis and reﬂux
• Constipation
• Positioning requirements
• Frequent surgical procedures
• Seizure disorder
• Use of multiple medications
• Sensory deﬁcits
• Caregiver knowledge/skill
• Resources including access to food
• Dental problems
